description_top: A chat system that never loses a message and never shows one twice, for a billion users. A full mock system design round at the Staff bar (L6/L7): interviewer, candidate and coach, {DURATION} minutes, {SLIDES} numbered slides, then {FOLLOWUPS} follow-ups.

The thesis: start from the mailbox, not the socket. A message is durably stored in its conversation log, with a server-assigned sequence number, before anything is acknowledged. Every device then catches up by cursor. The WebSocket only delivers early.

IN THIS ROUND
• Estimates as arithmetic: 100 M sockets, 20 PB a year, the million-receipt trap
• Wire formats for send, deliver and sync
• Data model: Chen ERD, physical tables, wide-column, hot keys and who writes them
• C4 context, container and component diagrams; a sequence and code for each path
• Ordering: one authority per conversation, and leader failover without reordering
• The lost ACK: every crash point, and why dedup comes before numbering
• Groups: shared log vs inbox copies, coalesced inbox writes, receipts as cursors
• A gateway dies with 500 k connections: jitter, resumption, admission control
• Edit and delete as a mid-round requirement; versioning a protocol for slow-updating phones

HOW TO USE IT
Watch once straight through. On the second pass, pause after each question and answer first. Slides badged AUX are the manager layer: skip them in a Staff round.

Numbers are back-of-the-envelope estimates for the exercise, not any company's real figures, and this is not any company's actual design.

post: A chat system that never loses a message and never shows one twice. How would you design it for a billion users?
I've published a {DURATION}-minute mock system design round at the Staff bar: interviewer, candidate and coach, on {SLIDES} numbered slides.

The idea that unlocks it: start from the mailbox, not the socket. Store the message durably, with a server-assigned sequence number, before anything is acknowledged. Every device then catches up by cursor. Online, offline and multi-device become one code path. The WebSocket only delivers early.

What the round goes into:
→ Who decides the order when two people send at once, and what happens when that leader dies mid-write
→ The lost ACK: every crash point, and why dedup has to come before numbering
→ The million-receipt trap in a group of 1,000, found with arithmetic
→ Half a million sockets reconnecting at once
→ Wire formats, C4 and sequence diagrams, the data model and code for each path
→ {FOLLOWUPS} follow-ups, from end-to-end encryption to a channel with a million subscribers
Attached: the full written design, 53 pages. Every decision with its alternatives, the arithmetic, the failure cases, and the internals of each tool.

▶ The video: {YOUTUBE_URL}

Best on a second pass: pause after each question and answer it first.
It's a scripted mock with synthetic voices, built with Claude Code from design-room, my open-source system design interview simulator. More rounds are coming, one problem at a time.
